sec.title: Background
sec.p: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) remains an aggressive disease with limited response to systemic therapies despite androgen deprivation. Immune-excluded prostate tumors are typically resistant to immunotherapy. STAR0602 is a selective bifunctional T-cell agonist composed of an antibody targeting Vβ6 and Vβ10 T-cell receptor chains fused to human interleukin-2 that selectively expands Vβ6+ CD8+ memory T cells and has demonstrated clinical activity as a monotherapy in anti-programmed death-ligand 1-resistant tumors (NCT05592626). We hypothesized that combining poly ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibition with Vβ-directed T-cell activation would enhance antitumor immunity and promote polyclonal T-cell responses in immune-excluded prostate cancer.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The antitumor activity of the PARP inhibitor olaparib combined with mSTAR1302, the murine surrogate of STAR0602, was evaluated in TRAMP-C2 and RM-1 prostate tumor models. Tumor growth, survival, and immune responses were assessed by flow cytometry and functional depletion studies. The role of tumor-intrinsic TRAIL-R2 signaling was evaluated using a TRAIL-R2 knockout TRAMP-C2 model, and clinical relevance was explored by assessing TRAIL-R2 expression in tumor samples from patients treated with olaparib in a Phase 2 clinical trial (NCT02484404).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 induced significant tumor regression and improved survival compared with either agent alone. Treatment increased tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, expanded activated Vβ13+ CD4+ and Vβ13+ CD8+ T cells, reduced immunosuppressive populations, and enriched stem-like progenitor exhausted CD8+ T cells. Depletion studies demonstrated that Vβ13+ CD4+ T cells, Vβ13+ CD8+ T cells, natural killer cells, and interferon-γ were required for therapeutic efficacy. TRAIL-R2 knockout experiments demonstrated that tumor-intrinsic TRAIL-R2 signaling contributes to the antitumor activity of the combination. Mechanistically, these findings support a model in which PARP inhibition sensitizes tumors while mSTAR1302-mediated Vβ13+ T-cell expansion initiates a broader polyclonal antitumor immune response associated with antigen spreading and recognition of multiple tumor antigens and neoepitopes.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These findings suggest that combining tumor-sensitizing therapies with selective T-cell activation may represent a broader strategy to overcome immune exclusion in solid tumors. Together, these results provide mechanistic rationale for clinical evaluation of olaparib in combination with STAR0602 in patients with mCRPC who have progressed on androgen deprivation therapy.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Olaparib is Food and Drug Administration approved as monotherapy or in combination with androgen deprivation therapy for the treatment of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) with BRCA mutations; however, improvement in overall survival remains an unmet need.

STAR0602 is a selective, bifunctional T-cell agonist that selectively expands specific Vβ6+ CD8+ memory T cells. Its murine surrogate, mSTAR1302, has shown antitumor activity as monotherapy across different tumor models.

This study showed for the first time that combination therapy with olaparib plus mSTAR1302 elicited significant tumor regression and survival benefit in two immune-excluded murine prostate cancer models. The antitumor response was associated with a decrease in immunosuppressive cells, an increase in activated Vβ13+ CD4+ and Vβ13+ CD8+ T cells, and an increase in the progenitor-exhausted CD8+ T-cell population. Vβ13+ CD4+ and Vβ13+ CD8+ T cells, as well as natural killer cells, are required for the antitumor efficacy observed by combination therapy with olaparib plus mSTAR1302.
Functional depletion studies demonstrated that Vβ13+ T cells contribute to the induction of downstream antigen-spreading responses and broader polyclonal antitumor immunity.
TRAIL-R2 upregulation modulated by olaparib is critical for the antitumor efficacy elicited by combination therapy with olaparib plus mSTAR1302.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: The ongoing Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating STAR0602 demonstrated expanded pan-tumor single-agent activity, with 59% of patients experiencing target-lesion tumor regression. Our study provides the rationale supporting the design of a clinical trial evaluating the combination of olaparib plus STAR0602 for patients with mCRPC who have progressed on androgen deprivation therapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) is an advanced disease stage that shows an aggressive phenotype associated with high mortality and morbidity.14 Currently, the first-line and second-line treatments for mCRPC use a combination of androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSIs) alone or in combination with poly ADP-ribose polymerase inhibitors (PARPis), taxanes, or radioligand therapy.1 2 5 In addition, current guidelines in prostate cancer recommend genetic testing for all men who present with metastatic disease to identify genetic mutations, including in DNA damage repair (DDR) genes, to inform the use of targeted therapies that can enhance treatment efficacy.4 6 7 Among DDR genes, the most clinically relevant are the homologous recombination repair (HRR) genes, with 20–25% of men with mCRPC carrying germline and/or somatic mutations in HRR genes.8 9

The higher prevalence of HRR alterations in advanced prostate cancer has yielded therapeutic strategies with PARPi. The Phase 3 PROfound (NCT02987543) and TRITON2 (NCT02558231) trials assessed PARPis olaparib and rucaparib monotherapy, respectively, in patients with mCRPC.10 11 Based on the results of the randomized, double-blind Phase 3 PROpel study of olaparib plus abiraterone vs placebo in mCRPC (NCT03732820), the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the PARPi olaparib plus abiraterone/prednisone for the treatment of patients with BRCA-mutated mCRPC.1 12 The PROpel study met its primary endpoint, demonstrating a statistically significant improvement in radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS)12; however, it failed to show an improvement in overall survival (OS),12 highlighting that even though these novel combination therapies have improved the mCRPC treatment landscape,1 2 4 13 there remains an unmet need for further treatment options, including combination therapies in advanced prostate cancer with PARPi.

Immunotherapy has shown limited clinical benefit in CRPC, particularly in light of recent setbacks with programmed death 1 (PD-1) plus PARPi combinations, such as the Phase 3 KEYLYNK-010 trial evaluating pembrolizumab (Keytruda) with olaparib (Lynparza). To address the inherent resistance of CRPC to immune checkpoint blockade, alternative strategies that actively stimulate or reprogram antitumor immunity may be warranted. The use of antibodies to selectively expand specific Vβ T-cell subsets, thereby modulating the germline T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire, represents a novel modality for T-cell activation.14 STAR0602 is a first-in-class bifunctional antibody targeting germline Vβ6/Vβ10 TCRs fused to human interleukin (IL)-2; thus engaging a non-clonal mode of TCR activation with cytokine co-stimulation in Vβ6/Vβ10+ subsets of T cells14 15 that are present at a high frequency relative to other Vβ subsets in tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) across several cancer types.14 15 STAR0602 is currently being evaluated as monotherapy in a multicenter Phase 1/2 clinical trial (NCT05592626).16 17 Preliminary results from that clinical study demonstrated activation and expansion of Vβ6 and Vβ10 TCR-expressing CD4+ and CD8+ effector memory (EM) T cells, as well as antitumor activity across seven major solid tumor types in heavily pretreated patients with both primary and secondary PD-1-resistant tumors.16 17 Particularly, pan-tumor monotherapy activity was observed in microsatellite stable and microsatellite instability (MSI)-high tumors across a range of tumor mutational burden (TMB) levels, irrespective of MSI status.16 17

PARP inhibition, specifically with olaparib, has been shown to induce CD8+ T-cell recruitment and activation in vivo,18 and the use of PARPis in many solid tumors is associated with neoantigen production and increased TMB due to the accumulation of cytoplasmic DNA fragments.19 In addition, our group demonstrated olaparib-mediated upregulation of TRAIL-R2 in both BRCA wild-type and BRCA mutant human prostate cancer cells, thereby increasing tumor cell sensitivity to natural killer (NK) killing.20 Previously, analysis of 9,142 The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) samples across 29 cancer types demonstrated that TCRβ variable gene (TRβV) usage patterns are broadly similar across multiple tumor types, including prostate.15 Hence, we aimed to exploit the immunomodulatory effect of olaparib to promote TRAIL-R2-mediated apoptosis and T-cell recruitment by expanding the Vβ13+ T-cell subsets throughout the administration of the murine surrogate of STAR0602, mSTAR130214 (online supplemental figure S1). Our studies were modeled to support the rationale for a clinical trial testing combination therapy with olaparib and STAR0602 as a second-line treatment for prostate cancer patients who failed the standard of care (SOC) of olaparib plus abiraterone/prednisone. To this end, we tested combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 in two different immune-excluded syngeneic prostate tumor models, TRAMP-C2 and RM-1. Here, we demonstrated for the first time that combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 elicited a robust tumor regression and improved survival benefit in both models. Specifically, in the TRAMP-C2 tumor model, it promoted CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell infiltration and proliferation of the targeted Vβ13+ population with central memory (CM)6 and EM phenotypes. In addition, our study demonstrates upregulation of TRAIL-R2 in murine prostate cancer cells following olaparib treatment and in ovarian carcinoma cells from biopsies of patients enrolled in a clinical study (NCT02484404) who received olaparib. Although the IL-2 arm has the potential to increase the regulatory T cell (Treg) population,21 no increase in Tregs was observed in the tumor or the periphery after combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302. Furthermore, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 triggered epitope spreading involving several known tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) and a neoantigen, indicating that the combination allows the expansion and evolution of the antitumor immune response (online supplemental figure S1). One major hurdle in cancer immunotherapy is T-cell exhaustion due to prolonged stimulation of the tumor antigen,22 and progenitor exhausted CD8+ T cells, known as progenitor-exhausted T (Tpex) cells, have been described as crucial to sustain an antitumor immune response, based on their robust self-renewal and proliferative abilities.22 23 Here, we demonstrated that combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed the potential to inhibit T-cell exhaustion by expanding the specific CD8+ Vβ13+ Tpex population. Altogether, these preclinical data support the rationale for combining olaparib with the bifunctional antibody STAR0602 in the clinical setting to improve the therapeutic outcome of patients with mCRPC who have failed androgen deprivation therapies.

sec.title: Combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 induces tumor regression in murine “cold” prostate cancer models
sec.p: Based on the immunomodulatory effect of olaparib previously discussed and the FDA approval of olaparib in men with mCRPC with germline or somatic HRR gene alterations who had disease progression while receiving enzalutamide or abiraterone,12 we chose to combine olaparib with mSTAR1302, which has shown to induce durable tumor regression across six murine solid tumor models.14 Combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 was tested in the murine prostate cancer models TRAMP-C2 and RM-1, which are both described in the literature as immunologically “cold” tumors.24

For the TRAMP-C2 model, olaparib treatment began at an average tumor volume of approximately 100 mm³ (day 20) and was administered intraperitoneally daily until the end of the study. The first mSTAR1302 dose was given after 5 days of olaparib treatment and subsequent doses of mSTAR1302 were given 1 week apart for a total of three doses (figure 1A). TRAMP-C2 tumor-bearing mice treated with olaparib (p<0.0001), mSTAR1302 (p<0.0001), or combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (p<0.0001; figure 1B) showed a significant antitumor efficacy compared with mice treated with vehicle. Combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 outperformed olaparib and mSTAR1302 monotherapies, showing a sustained significant antitumor efficacy (p<0.0001, p=0.0001; figure 1B). Furthermore, after three doses of mSTAR1302 on day 61, in mice receiving olaparib or mSTAR1302 alone, the average tumor volume was four times (255 mm3) and 3.7 times higher (227 mm3) than the average tumor volume of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (62 mm3) (figure 1C). This highlights the benefit of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 over monotherapies. In this model, mice in each treatment group showed no toxicity (online supplemental figure S2).

sec.p: All treatments tested showed a survival benefit. Compared with mice in the vehicle group, olaparib (p=0.007), mSTAR1302 (p=0.002), and combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (p=0.001; figure 1D) increased median OS. Notably, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 significantly improved survival compared with mSTAR1302 alone (p=0.003; figure 1D) and to olaparib (p=0.002; figure 1D), with a median OS of 97 days versus 77 days in both monotherapies (figure 1D).

Single agents and combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 were also tested in an alternative schedule. In this schedule, the first mSTAR1302 dose was given at the start of olaparib treatment, when tumors were around 100 mm3 (online supplemental figure S3A). This schedule showed no advantage in antitumor efficacy in combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 compared with mSTAR1302 alone (p=0.06; online supplemental figure S3B); therefore, no further studies were pursued using this schedule. Next, we confirmed the targeting of the Vβ13+ T population by combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 in the TRAMP-C2 mouse model. For this, the spleens of mice in all treatment groups were harvested, and single-cell suspensions were stained and analyzed by flow cytometry 3 days after the first mSTAR1302 dose (day 27). Spleens of mice in mSTAR1302 alone (p<0.001, p<0.001) and combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (p<0.001, p<0.001; figure 1E) groups showed two times the percentage of CD4+ Vβ13+ T cells (40%) observed in vehicle (20%) and olaparib (20%) groups. Likewise, mSTAR1302 alone (p<0.0001, p<0.0001) and combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (p<0.0001, p<0.0001; figure 1F) groups showed three times the percentage of CD8+ Vβ13+ T cells (60%) observed in vehicle (20%) and olaparib (20%) groups. The data confirm that mSTAR1302, as a single agent or in combination with olaparib, expands the Vβ13+ T-cell population. In contrast, negligible percentages (0%–2.5%) of CD4+ Vβ5+ (figure 1G), CD4+ Vβ11+ (figure 1H), CD8+ Vβ5+ (figure 1I), and CD8+ Vβ11+ T cells (figure 1J) were observed in the spleens of mice in mSTAR1302 alone or combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 groups, respectively. These findings suggest that mSTAR1302 did not cross-react with the other Vβ T-cell populations tested.

To better understand the effect of the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 on the Vβ13+ T-cell population, the proliferation capacity of this T-cell subset in the peripheral blood was assessed in TRAMP-C2 tumor-bearing mice alive in all groups at day 76 of the study. At this time, all mice in the vehicle group have reached ethical limits; hence, euthanasia was performed. Mice in combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed a fivefold increase in the number of CD4+ (p=0.005, p=0.001; online supplemental figure S4A) and CD8+ (p=0.001, p=0.001; online supplemental figure S4D) T cells compared with olaparib and mSTAR1302 alone. Consistently, CD4+ Vβ13+ (p=0.004, p=0.001; online supplemental figure S4B) and CD8+ Vβ13+ (p=0.001, p=0.001; online supplemental figure S4E) T-cell subsets showed a fivefold increase compared with olaparib and mSTAR1302 alone. Combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 promoted a proliferative phenotype of CD4+ Vβ13+ Ki67+ (p=0.012, p=0.002; online supplemental figure S4C) and CD8+ Vβ13+ Ki67+ (p=0.0350, p=0.004; online supplemental figure S4F) T-cell subsets compared with olaparib and mSTAR1302 alone.

Single agents and the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 were also tested in the RM-1 model following the treatment schedule shown in online supplemental figure S5 to assess both antitumor efficacy and survival benefit. In this model, mice treated with olaparib (p=0.018), mSTAR1302 (p<0.0001), or combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (p<0.0001; figure 1K) exhibited significant tumor inhibition compared with mice treated with vehicle alone. In terms of survival benefit, our study showed that combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 significantly increased survival compared with vehicle (p<0.0001), olaparib (p<0.0001), and mSTAR1302 (p=0.033; figure 1L), with a median OS of 24 days. Similar to the TRAMP-C2 model, no toxicity was observed based on mouse body weight across any treatment group. Like the TRAMP-C2 model, mSTAR1302, as a single agent or in combination with olaparib, expanded the Vβ13+ T-cell population (figure 1M,N) and has no off-target effects on other Vβ T cells, such as Vβ5+ and Vβ11+ (1%; figure 1O,P,Q,R). Overall, these data showed the strong antitumor effect of the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 in promoting the regression of two different “cold” murine prostate tumors.

sec.title: Combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 induces lymphocyte infiltration in an immune-excluded tumor and a differential gene signaling promoting an activated and cytotoxic T-cell phenotype
sec.p: To further explore the potential mechanisms driving the antitumor efficacy observed with combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302, we sought to identify the immune cells involved and the changes in tumor gene signatures. RNA analysis was performed on the TRAMP-C2 model using the nCounter murine PanCancer Immune Profiling Panel on individual tumors harvested from each treatment group on day 27, which was 3 days after the first mSTAR1302 dose and 7 days of olaparib treatment. The RNA analysis showed an enrichment in cytotoxic cells, CD8+ T cells, macrophages, NK cells, and dendritic cells in tumors of mice treated with the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (figure 2A). In contrast, immunosuppressive Treg populations were diminished (figure 2A). Gene expression analysis showed that in tumors of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302, genes associated with activation such as granzyme A, granzyme B (Gzmb), and perforin were upregulated and genes associated with promoting immune suppression such as Tgfb2 and Foxp3 were downregulated (figure 2B). In addition, Ingenuity Pathway Analysis illustrated that tumors from mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed an average of 3.3-fold upregulation of signaling pathways associated with T-cell activation, antigen (Ag) presentation, immune homeostasis and immune response, compared with tumors of mice receiving olaparib or mSTAR1302 alone (figure 2C).

sec.p: Flow cytometry analysis was performed on tumors from mice in all treatment groups to assess TILs. Combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed a marked increase in the number of CD45+ CD3+ cells per milligram of tumor compared with vehicle (p=0.005), olaparib (p=0.044), and mSTAR1302 (p=0.045; figure 2D) cohorts. In addition, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 increased CD4+ T-cell infiltration compared with vehicle (p=0.036) and mSTAR1302 (p=0.048; figure 2E) cohorts. On the other hand, a significant increase in CD8+ T cells was observed in tumors of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 compared with vehicle (p=0.003) and olaparib (p=0.025; figure 3F) cohorts. In tumors from mice of any group, no significant increase in the CD4+ Vβ13+ subset was observed (figure 2G); however, there was an increase in CD8+ Vβ13+ T-cell infiltration in the tumors of mice that received combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 compared with vehicle (p=0.001) and olaparib alone (p=0.019; figure 2H).

sec.p: Besides the transcriptomic and flow cytometry data, immunofluorescence staining confirmed the enrichment of TILs in mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (figure 2I). CD4+ (p<0.0001, p=0.001, p=0.005; figure 2J) and CD8+ T cells (p<0.0001, p=0.001, p<0.0001; figure 2K) were significantly higher in mice in combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 group compared with mice in vehicle, olaparib, and mSTAR1302 alone cohorts. Overall, these findings expand on how combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 increases immune cell infiltration and enhances a diverse cytotoxic immune response.

sec.title: Activated cytotoxic T cells and NK cells are sustained in the periphery by combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302
sec.p: To interrogate the activation status of immune cells in the periphery of the treated mice, the expression of activation markers was assessed. Mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed high proliferation of activated CD4+ Vβ13+ T cells compared with mice in the vehicle group, confirmed by Ki67 (p<0.001; figure 3A), GzmB (p<0.001; figure 3B), and interferon (IFN)-γ (p=0.001; figure 3C) markers. Similarly, a population of activated CD8+ Vβ13+ T cells was confirmed in the combination therapy group, as shown by Ki67 (p<0.0001; figure 3D), GzmB (p<0.001; figure 3E), IFN-γ (p<0.001; figure 3F) markers, as well as the presence of double-positive GzmB, IFN-γ CD8+ Vβ13+ T cells (p<0.001; figure 3G). In addition, our study demonstrated that mSTAR1302 alone resulted in a significant increase in CM (p<0.001; figure 3H) and EM CD8+ T cells (p<0.001; figure 3I) compared with vehicle group. Likewise, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 significantly increased CD8+ CM T cells (p=0.017; figure 3J) and CD8+ EM T cells (p=0.001; figure 3K) compared with the vehicle group. However, only combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 resulted in a significant increase in CD8+ Vβ13+ CM (p<0.001; figure 3J) and CD8+ Vβ13+ EM T-cell subsets (p<0.001; figure 3K) compared with mSTAR1302 alone.

Since T cell and NK cell activities are intertwined functions of the adaptive and innate immune responses, cytokines (ie, tumor microenvironment-α and IFN-γ) secreted by activated NK cells can promote a stimulus response in the activation and proliferation of T cells.25 A significant increase in NK cells was observed in the spleens of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 compared with all treatment groups (p<0.001, p<0.001, p<0.001; figure 3L). Moreover, GzmB+ NK cells confirmed their activated status compared with vehicle (p<0.001) and olaparib alone (p<0.001; figure 3M) groups. In addition, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding analysis helped visualize the negligible numbers of NK cells in vehicle and olaparib groups compared with the increased numbers of NK cells in the mSTAR1302 and combination therapy groups (figure 3N). In summary, the data confirmed that combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 promotes an activated phenotype, which is expected to foster a long-lasting antitumor effect.

sec.title: Combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 elicits a reduction of immune-suppressive cells and the expansion of a cytotoxic T-cell pool
sec.p: Next, the myeloid compartment was interrogated to assess the status of immunosuppressive populations. The spleens of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed a significant increase in M1 macrophages compared with mice in the vehicle group (p=0.048; figure 4A). Along with this finding, a significant decrease in M2 macrophages (p=0.014; figure 4B), monocyte-myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSC) (p=0.001; figure 4C), and Tregs (p=0.044; figure 4E) was observed in mice treated with combination therapy in the olaparib and mSTAR1302 group compared with mice in the vehicle group.

TRAMP-C2 cells (2.5×106 cells/mL, 1:1 Matrigel) were implanted in male C57BL/6 mice (8–12 weeks old; n=8–10/group) and treated as described in figure 1A. On day 27, spleens were isolated and stained for flow analysis for (A) M1 (CD38+ CD206−), (B) M2 (CD38Low CD206+), (C) M-MDSC (Ly6C+ Ly6G−), (D) G-MDSC (Ly6CLow Ly6G+), and (E) Tregs (FoxP3+ CD25+). Tumors were harvested, and TILs were isolated and stained for flow analysis for (F) total macrophages, (G) M1, (H) M2, (I) M-MDSC, (J) G-MDSC, (K) Tpex (PD-1+ TCF-1+ CD62L+), and (L) Vβ13+ Tpex. (M) Representative plot of Vβ13+ Tpex population, (N) exhausted CD8+ and (O) exhausted CD8+ Vβ13+ T-cell populations. Tumors were processed in PBS, and tumor lysates from all groups were collected for O-link proteomic analysis. Plots showing quantification of soluble (P) PD-L1 (CD274) and (Q) CTLA-4. This experiment was conducted two times, with similar results. The data shown are representative of one experiment. One-way ANOVA measured significance with Tukey’s multiple comparison test. *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001, and ****p<0.0001. sec.p: In contrast to the spleens, tumors from mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed a significant decrease in total macrophages (p=0.005; figure 4F) and M1 macrophage population (p=0.001, p=002, p=0.012; figure 4G) compared with mice in vehicle, olaparib, and mSTAR1302 groups, respectively. However, the M2 macrophage population was significantly decreased in mice treated with combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 compared with vehicle (p<0.0001) and olaparib alone (p<0.0001; figure 4H). Along with these findings, the immunosuppressive populations of M-MDSC (p=0.007, p=0.003; figure 4I) and granulocyte-MDSC (p=0.005, p=0.003; figure 4J) were significantly suppressed by the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 compared with vehicle and olaparib alone.

In terms of the Tpex cell population, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 significantly increased this subset compared with vehicle, olaparib, and mSTAR1302 groups (p=0.001, p=0.024, p=0.014, respectively; figure 4K). An increase in Vβ13+ Tpex population was observed in tumors of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 compared with mice in vehicle and olaparib groups (p=0.015, p=0.021, respectively; figure 4L,M), highlighting the capability of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 in maintaining a pool of self-renewing specific CD8+ Vβ13+ T cells. In addition, TILs isolated from tumors of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed a significant decrease in exhausted CD8+ (p=0.007; figure 4N) and CD8+ Vβ13+ T-cell populations (p=0.019; figure 4O) compared with mSTAR1302 alone. These results are aligned with the significant decrease of the soluble inhibitory ligands programmed death-ligand 1 (CD274) (p=0.001; figure 4P) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (p=0.022; figure 4Q) in mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 compared with mSTAR1302 alone. Altogether, these data underscore the potential of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 to diminish exhausted CD8+ T cells and immune-suppressive cells, while maintaining a pool of self-renewing CD8+ T cells in the tumor.

sec.title: Vβ13+ CD4+, Vβ13+ CD8+ T cells, and NK cells are required to drive the antitumor and antigen cascade response elicited by combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302
sec.p: To determine the specific immune cells required for the enhanced antitumor efficacy of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 in the TRAMP-C2 prostate cancer model, we depleted CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, Vβ13+ T-cell subset, and NK cells. Selective depletion of CD4+ (p<0.001) and CD8+ T cells (p=0.004; figure 5A) significantly lessened the ability of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 to suppress TRAMP-C2 tumor growth. Similarly, depletion of the Vβ13+ T-cell subset (p=0.047; figure 5A) significantly diminished the antitumor efficacy of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302. The abrogation of the antitumor efficacy of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302, with the depletion of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and the Vβ13+ T-cell subset, is in accordance with our findings of these immune cells being significantly high in the peripheral blood of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (online supplemental figure S4A,B,D,E). Furthermore, depletion of NK cells significantly diminished the antitumor efficacy of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (p<0.001; figure 5A). Concurrent depletion of CD4+, CD8+, and Vβ13+ T cells and NK cells also abrogated the antitumor efficacy of the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (p<0.001; figure 5A).

sec.p: The requirement of T cells (CD4+, CD8+, and Vβ13+) and NK cells for the observed antitumor efficacy in combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 raised the question of how crucial IFN-γ was to the antitumor activity. Hence, IFN-γ levels were determined in serum and tumor lysates of mice in all groups. The mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed a significant increase in IFN-γ levels, in both serum (p<0.0001, p<0.0001; figure 5B) and tumor lysates (p<0.001, p=0.004; figure 5B), compared with olaparib and mSTAR1302 alone. Additionally, the requirement of IFN-γ was confirmed when IFN-γ depletion abrogated the tumor regression elicited by the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (p=0.001; figure 5C).

To determine Ag-specific responses elicited by each treatment, splenocytes from mice in all groups were stimulated in vitro with major histocompatibility complex class I H-2Db- or H-2Kb-restricted peptide epitopes for p15E, an endogenous retroviral tumor Ag; Twist, a transcription factor associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)26; stimulator of prostatic adenocarcinoma-specific T cells-1 wild-type (SPAS-1 WT), the first T cell-defined TRAMP tumor Ag27; or SPAS-1 mutant (SPAS-1 MUT).28 SPAS-1 MUT neo-Ag arose from a point mutation in one allele of the SPAS-1 gene, replacing the amino acid arginine with histidine at position 8 (SNC9-H8).27 For p15e, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed a significant increase of IFN-γ-producing CD8+ T cells compared with olaparib (p=0.001) and mSTAR1302 (p=0.008; figure 5D) groups. Spleens harvested from mice in the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 group and stimulated with Twist peptide showed a significant increase of IFN-γ-producing CD8+ T cells compared with olaparib (p=0.015) and mSTAR1302 (p=0.021; figure 5E) groups. Recognition of the SPAS-1 WT TAA by CD8+ T cells of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 was confirmed (p=0.021, p=0.021, p=0.028; figure 5F). Finally, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 significantly increased IFN-γ-producing CD8+ T cells targeting SPAS-1 MUT neo-Ag compared with olaparib (p=0.006) and mSTAR1302 (p=0.040; figure 5G). To further interrogate the functional role of Vβ13 T cells, splenocytes from TRAMP-C2 tumor-bearing mice treated with vehicle, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302, or a Vβ13-depleting antibody prior to combination therapy were stimulated with previously described TAAs and neo-Ag peptide epitopes. Consistent with previous findings (figure 5A), depletion of Vβ13 T cells significantly diminished the antitumor efficacy of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (p=0.007; figure 5H). Enzyme-Linked ImmunoSpot (ELISpot) analysis showed again that combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 generated a robust IFN-γ response against TAAs, p15E (p=0.022; figure 5I), Twist (p=0.008; figure 5J), and SPAS-1 WT (p=0.001; figure 5K) and neo-Ag SPAS-1 MUT compared with vehicle group (p=0.041; figure 5L). Importantly, mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 plus depletion of Vβ13 T cells markedly reduced IFN-γ responses to p15E (p=0.024; figure 5I), Twist (p=0.003; figure 5J), SPAS-1 WT (p=0.001; figure 5K) and SPAS-1 MUT (p=0.048; figure 5L) compared with combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302.

Altogether, these findings strongly support the requirement for CD4+, CD8+, and Vβ13+ T cells, NK cells, and IFN-γ, secreted mainly by these immune cells, for the antitumor efficacy observed with combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302. Moreover, these findings confirm that olaparib plus mSTAR1302 combination therapy promotes epitope spreading and support the hypothesis that certain “off-the-shelf” agents may trigger and enable patients to produce their own “neoepitope vaccine”.29

sec.title: Upregulation of TRAIL-R2 on TRAMP-C2 cells by olaparib is critical for antitumor efficacy
sec.p: To evaluate the role of olaparib in promoting the antitumor efficacy elicited by combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 in the TRAMP-C2 model, phenotypic changes were determined in TRAMP-C2 cells after olaparib treatment (20 µM) in vitro, and the treated cells were analyzed by flow cytometry. The analysis revealed that death-receptor TRAIL-R2 was significantly upregulated following olaparib treatment compared with untreated cells (p=0.01; figure 6A). To confirm the role of TRAIL-R2 in sensitizing TRAMP-C2 cells to killing, we performed functional in vitro and in vivo assays. For the in vitro assay, the percentage of lysis was determined in pretreated TRAMP-C2 cells after the addition of a soluble recombinant form of TRAIL, known as KillerTRAIL, allowing assessment of cell sensitivity to TRAIL-mediated apoptosis. There, olaparib-treated TRAMP-C2 cells plus KillerTRAIL showed a significantly higher percentage of lysis (28%) compared with untreated cells plus KillerTRAIL (15%; p<0.005) and compared with cells treated with olaparib alone (11%; p=0.001; figure 6B). Recapitulating a portion of the data presented in figure 1B, TRAMP-C2 tumor-bearing mice treated with combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed a significant tumor regression compared with mice treated with vehicle (p<0.001) and olaparib (p<0.001) and mSTAR1302 monotherapies (p=0.001; figure 6C).

sec.p: To expand on the contribution of TRAIL-R2 in TRAMP-C2 cells’ sensitization to killing, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated TRAIL-R2 knockout (KO) was performed (figure 6D), followed by the functional assay using KillerTRAIL and an in vivo experiment. Olaparib-treated TRAIL-R2 KO cells plus KillerTRAIL (8%) showed no enhancement in the percentage of cell lysis compared with untreated cells plus KillerTRAIL (8%) and compared with cells treated with olaparib alone (10%; figure 6E). Additionally, TRAIL-R2 KO TRAMP-C2 cells were implanted in mice and treated as previously described in figure 1A. In contrast to what was observed in the TRAMP-C2 WT model (figure 6C), the antitumor activity achieved by combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 was markedly diminished compared with vehicle (p=0.06), to olaparib (p=0.783) and to mSTAR1302 (p=0.380; figure 6F) single agent-treated mice. In summary, these data support the hypothesis that olaparib modulates TRAIL-R2 upregulation in TRAMP-C2 tumor cells, and that TRAIL-mediated apoptosis contributes in part to the antitumor efficacy of the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302.

sec.title: TRAIL-R2 has low expression in ovarian or prostate cancer compared with healthy tissue but is induced by olaparib in patients with ovarian cancer
sec.p: Based on previous findings showing upregulation of TRAIL-R2 in BRCA-mutated and wild-type human prostate cancer cell lines after olaparib treatment,20 we sought clinical relevance by first interrogating TRAIL-R2 expression in human prostate and ovarian tissue from cancer and healthy patients using TCGA and solid tissue Genotype-Tissue Expression datasets. TRAIL-R2 transcript expression was significantly decreased in patients with prostate cancer tissue (p<0.001; figure 7A) and in patients with ovarian cancer tissue (p<0.001; figure 7B) when compared with their healthy donor counterparts.

sec.p: Next, we evaluated whether PARP inhibition with olaparib could induce TRAIL-R2 upregulation in the patient tumors. We used available in-house clinical samples from a Phase 2 trial (NCT02484404), which enrolled women with recurrent ovarian cancer with measurable disease (per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) V.1.1), because no fresh biopsies were available from patients with prostate cancer treated with olaparib. This clinical trial aimed to confirm preclinical data, suggesting an immunostimulatory effect of PARP inhibition in the ovarian cancer microenvironment.30

Using paired fresh core biopsies from three patients with ovarian cancer enrolled in this study, we found that ovarian cancer tissue post-olaparib treatment showed a significant upregulation in TRAIL-R2 expression compared with ovarian cancer tissue pre-olaparib treatment (p=0.001, p=0.001, and p<0.001, respectively; figure 7C). In summary, the upregulation of TRAIL-R2 in ovarian biopsies post-olaparib treatment supported the rationale for designing a clinical trial combining olaparib with the novel TCR Vβ-targeted bifunctional antibody STAR0602.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Over the last decade, mCRPC treatment has evolved from chemotherapy to multimodal approaches that include ARSIs, targeted molecular therapies, selected immunotherapies, and radioligand therapy.3 4 Several of these agents are currently under clinical development or have been approved in combination with other agents for the treatment of patients with mCRPC. However, limited OS gains and persistent resistance mechanisms continue to challenge the efficacy of PARP inhibition as monotherapy or in combination.10 12 31 In general, targeting the TCR region with antibodies has proven effective for activating T cells and clearing tumors.32 33 However, toxicity profiles, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS), remain a primary concern for T cell-activating therapies.3436 Since STAR0602 targets only a small subset of the T-cell compartment, limited CRS was observed in non-human primates compared with dosing with non-selective TCR agonists, such as anti-CD3 T-cell engagers.14 37 Additionally, manageable CRS was reported in preliminary data from a Phase 1/2 clinical trial of intravenous STAR0602 in human subjects who received no CRS prophylaxis medications.16 Initial results from the Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating STAR0602 as monotherapy have shown a 20% objective response rate and an 80% disease control rate in TMB-high (TMB-H) tumors, including colorectal, lung, breast, gastric, head and neck, and bladder cancers.17

The current study confirmed and extended previous data illustrating the antitumor efficacy of the murine version of STAR0602, mSTAR1302, as a single agent across several syngeneic tumor models, and the activation and expansion of the Vβ13+ T-cell population.14 In our study, the combination of mSTAR1302 with the PARPi olaparib demonstrated a robust antitumor response with survival benefit in two different immune-excluded prostate cancer models (figure 1B–D,K,L), accompanied by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells tumor infiltration (figure 2E,F and I–K) and a sustained proliferation of the targeted Vβ13+ population (online supplemental figure S4A–F). The TRAMP-C2 and RM-1 tumor models were examined in the subcutaneous rather than orthotopic setting. These potential limitations will ultimately be addressed in a planned clinical trial evaluating olaparib plus STAR0602 in patients with mCRPC. PARP inhibition has been shown to increase immune cell infiltration at the tumor site by inhibiting the EMT, regulating nuclear factor-kappa B cells transcription factor, or activating the glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta pathway.19 38 Together, these results suggest that both agents, olaparib and mSTAR1302, contribute to the highly immune-infiltrated tumors in mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 compared with mSTAR1302 or olaparib monotherapies (figure 2I–K). Our study showed not only that combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 expanded Vβ13+ CD4+ and Vβ13+ CD8+ T cells expressing GzmB or IFN-γ (figure 3B,C,E,F), but also the expansion of Vβ13+ CD8+ T cells expressing both markers (figure 3G). GzmB-IFN-γ-producing CD8+ T cells often exhibit an enhanced cytotoxic profile; in colon cancer, this T-cell phenotype has been associated with modulation of the tumor microenvironment and a better prognosis.39 40 While in this study only the expansion of cytotoxic T lymphocytes was confirmed in the periphery (figure 3A–K) and not in the tumor, RNA analysis of tumors confirmed upregulation of T-cell activation signaling pathways, upregulation of proinflammatory cytokine genes, and the enrichment of cytotoxic cells and NK cells (figure 2A–C).

The bivalent binding of the mSTAR1302 molecule to both the Vβ13 TCR and IL-2 receptors is necessary for targeted T-cell subset activation.14 Combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 showed a sustained population of activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, as well as NK cells (figure 3B,C,E,F,G,L,M), and high levels of IFN-γ were confirmed in tumor lysates and serum of mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (figure 5B). The cross-regulation of IFN-γ and CD4+ T cells, as well as its role in enhancing Ag presentation and apoptosis induction, is well-documented41 42; hence, the loss of antitumor efficacy after selective depletion of CD4+, CD8+, Vβ13+ T cells, NK cells, as well as IFN-γ depletion (figure 5A,C). It was previously demonstrated in the EMT mammary tumor model that mSTAR1302 monotherapy induced significant tumor regression; however, this effect was abrogated when Vβ13 T cells were depleted prior to treatment.14 In figure 5A, we show that TRAMP-C2 mice treated with olaparib plus mSTAR1302 exhibited significant antitumor activity. Depletion of Vβ13 T cells significantly attenuated the therapeutic effect of the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302. We hypothesize that the antitumor activity of olaparib plus mSTAR1302 is not solely due to expansion of Vβ13 T cells; rather, expansion of Vβ13 T cells is a critical contributor to the induction of a polyclonal T-cell response, including responses to multiple TAAs and neoepitopes (online supplemental figure S1, figure 5D–G). Expanded Vβ13 T cells might support this polyclonal response through multiple molecular mechanisms and cytokine support, as evidenced by IFN-γ depletion, which reversed the antitumor activity of olaparib plus mSTAR1302 therapy (figure 5C). ELISpot studies performed following Vβ13 T-cell depletion shed light on one of the possible underlying mechanisms by providing evidence that Vβ13 T cells play a functional role in orchestrating downstream Ag cascade responses induced by combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (figure 5I–L). Specifically, depletion of Vβ13 T cells significantly reduced IFN-γ responses against the TAAs tested and the neoantigen SPAS-1 MUT, indicating that Vβ13 T cells contribute to the development of broader polyclonal antitumor immunity (figure 5H–L).

In mCRPC, a high percentage of myeloid-derived suppressor cells is associated with a shorter median OS.43 44 In our study, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 reduced the M-MDSC myeloid population, Tregs, and downregulated Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β)-signaling pathway and FoxP3 gene transcription (figure 2A–C; figure 4C,E,I,J). In the context of macrophage polarization, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 promoted a shift from the M2 to the M1 phenotype in the periphery (figure 4A,B). The high levels of IFN-γ observed in combination therapy (figure 5B,C) may have contributed to macrophage polarization,4547 and studies in prostate and breast cancers have shown that olaparib promotes polarization from M2 to M1 phenotype.48 49 The reduction in M2 macrophage population, both in the periphery and in the tumor, confirms the potency of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 in suppressing a phenotype that favors tumor progression (figure 4G,H). Additionally, other studies show that inhibition of PARP1 protein by olaparib can block the transcription of proinflammatory cytokines that promote the differentiation of tumor-associated macrophages into the M2 phenotype.19 50

Epitope spreading/Ag cascade and responses to neoepitopes have been strongly associated with improved therapeutic responses.5153 Herein, we demonstrated the capacity of combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 to generate IFN-γ-producing CD8+ T cells targeting multiple Ags: p15E, Twist, and SPAS-1 WT (figure 5D–G). Additionally, recognition of SPAS-1 MUT neo-Ag from mice receiving combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 suggests the long-term antitumor effect of combination therapy, as a study showed that mice immunized with the SNC9-H8 peptide (SPAS-1 MUT) gained CD8+ T cell-mediated protection against TRAMP-C2 rechallenge.54 Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the hypothesis that certain “off-the-shelf” agents may trigger and enable patients to produce their own “neoepitope” in situ.29 Combinations of these agents, such as olaparib plus mSTAR1302, have the potential to activate tumor-associated T-cell responses, enhance the immune response, and inhibit immunosuppressive cells, thereby improving therapeutic efficacy.29

CD8+ T-cell exhaustion is an inevitable consequence of chronic Ag exposure.55 Nonetheless, combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 has shown the potential to overcome T-cell exhaustion by expanding the Tpex population intratumorally (figure 4K–M). Tpex is a CD8+ T-cell subset that exhibits stem cell-like properties and influences the efficacy of immunotherapy.22 55 56 Even though Tpex cells lack effective cytotoxic functions and can develop into terminally exhausted T cells (Texterm), they possess a remarkable ability to transition into functional effector-exhausted CD8+ T cells (Texeff) with heightened expression of GzmB and IFN-γ.22 Thus, our study demonstrated that combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 promotes the expansion of a CD8+ T-cell pool with cytotoxic potential.

Several studies have demonstrated upregulation of TRAIL-R2 in various cancer cell lines at both the mRNA and protein levels following PARP inhibition, resulting in increased sensitivity to killing.20 57 58 The treatment schedule was important in the combination therapy with olaparib and mSTAR1302 (figure 1A, online supplemental figure S3). The difference in efficacy between the two schedules is likely due to pre-exposure to olaparib upregulating TRAIL-R2 (figure 6A), thereby enabling enhanced activity of Vβ13+ T cells induced by mSTAR1302. Here, we confirmed the upregulation of TRAIL-R2 in murine prostate cancer cells after olaparib treatment (figure 6A) and extended this finding to clinical data, where upregulation of TRAIL-R2 was also confirmed in tumor biopsies from patients with ovarian cancer after treatment with olaparib (figure 7C). Given the paucity of available fresh biopsies from patients with prostate cancer, particularly in patients with bone only disease, we opted to use ovarian cancer tumor biopsies to test our hypothesis in the clinical setting. In a planned clinical trial in patients with mCRPC receiving olaparib plus STAR0602, TRAIL-R2 will be interrogated in tissue biopsies to further elucidate its role in this cancer type. An enhanced sensitization of TRAMP-C2 prostate cancer cells to TRAIL-R2-mediated apoptosis was also confirmed in our in vitro and in vivo studies (figure 6B,C,E,F). The findings of our study support the rationale for combining olaparib, due to its ability to induce TRAIL-R2-mediated apoptosis, with the human version of mSTAR1302, which activates and expands Vβ13+ T-cell populations.

The clinical activity of PARPis in prostate cancer is most pronounced in BRCA-mutated and homologous recombination-deficient tumors. To our knowledge, neither the RM-1 nor the TRAMP-C2 murine prostate cancer cell line models have been characterized as BRCA-mutant or canonical HR-deficient. Studies evaluating the combination therapy of olaparib and mSTAR1302 in BRCA-mutant and PARPi-resistant models are currently under consideration. Olaparib in combination with the androgen biosynthesis inhibitor, abiraterone, was approved as an SOC therapy for patients with BRCA-mutated mCRPC after the PROpel Phase 3 clinical study showed improvement in rPFS receiving the combination.12 However, the study did not report an improvement in OS for these patients (median OS: 42.1 months vs 34.7 months; HR: 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.00; p = 0.0544).12 Therefore, the improvement in OS and quality of life of patients with mCRPC remains an unmet need. In summary, the preclinical data presented in this study support the translational potential of combining olaparib with the bifunctional antibody STAR0602 for patients with mCRPC who have failed first-line and second-line treatments. These findings suggest that expansion of Vβ13 T cells serves as a catalytic event that promotes Ag spreading and polyclonal antitumor immunity following PARP inhibition.
